narrative:
The model predicted an 88.2% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to assess likely success in law school and beyond, your application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Being in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) placed you far below the average ranking of accepted students (around 5.8), signaling consistent academic struggle in law school. Your first-year ranking was the third most important factor and also increased the chance of failure; a second-decile ranking is well below the typical sixth-decile performance of admitted students.

Your undergraduate GPA worked in the opposite direction. At 3.5 it is higher than the 3.23 average of accepted applicants and therefore pulled the prediction modestly toward passing. However, this positive signal was not large enough to offset the two weak class-rank signals.

Your LSAT score of 30 (versus an accepted-student average of 37), upper-middle family income, and plan to attend full-time played smaller roles and did not change the overall outlook.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance and retaking the LSAT to demonstrate stronger readiness. Consider reapplying once you have clearer evidence of ability to succeed in law school and on the bar exam. (218 words)
